spans.content: ScopusLit: An end-to-end Web-based tool for bibliometric analysis
Orlando Arroyo
Universidad Industrial de Santander, Bucaramanga, Santander, Colombia
A R T I C L E I N F O
Keywords:
Bibliometric analysis
Scopus
Systematic literature review
Topic modeling
A B S T R A C T
Bibliometric analysis supports systematic literature reviews, but it often requires disconnected tools for search,
data storage, analysis, visualization, and export. This paper presents ScopusLit, an open-source, browser-based
application for analyzing scientific literature indexed in Scopus through an integrated, zero-code workflow.
Developed in Python with Streamlit and pybliometrics, ScopusLit executes Scopus Advanced Search queries
through the API, retrieves abstracts, stores reproducible JSON datasets, and provides bibliometric, network, and
abstract-level text analyses. Its functionality is demonstrated using a search query that retrieved 1036 records in
52 s and downloaded abstracts with 100% success in 678 s. The example illustrates temporal, geographic,
keyword, co-occurrence, TF-IDF, and topic-modeling outputs, including network generation and NMF topic
modeling. By combining Scopus-based retrieval, analysis, consolidation, and publication-ready export in a single
web interface, ScopusLit reduces manual transfers between tools and supports reproducible bibliometric work-
flows for review-oriented research.

spans.content: 1. Motivation and significance
Bibliometric analysis is a cornerstone of systematic literature re-
views, research trend identification, and science mapping [1]. Re-
searchers frequently rely on the Scopus database, one of the largest
curated abstract and citation databases of peer-reviewed literature,
encompassing over 27,000 titles from >7000 publishers [2]. However,
conducting rigorous bibliometric studies typically requires combining
multiple disconnected tools: Scopus’s web interface for search, spread-
sheet software for data cleaning, specialized bibliometric software for
analysis, and graphic design tools for producing publication-quality
figures.
While several established tools facilitate these analyses, they often
present distinct limitations. For instance, VOSviewer [3] excels in the
network visualization of co-authorship, co-citation, and keyword
co-occurrence, yet it lacks text analysis capabilities and requires manual
data importation. Similarly, Bibliometrix [4] offers comprehensive
bibliometric indicators but demands proficiency in R programming.
Tools like CiteSpace [5] and Publish or Perish [6] also exhibit con-
straints, either by relying on manual file transfers or offering limited
visualization and text analysis capabilities. Consequently, none of these
alternatives provides an integrated, zero-code workflow that spans from
Scopus query execution to abstract-level text analysis. Conversely,
programmatic solutions such as the pybliometrics Python library [7]
offer robust API access but requires coding expertise, limiting accessi-
bility for non-programmers.

application designed for the comprehensive bibliometric analysis of
Scopus-indexed literature. Developed in Python using the Streamlit web

views, research trend identification, and science mapping [1]. Re-

curated abstract and citation databases of peer-reviewed literature,

conducting rigorous bibliometric studies typically requires combining
multiple disconnected tools: Scopus’s web interface for search, spread-
sheet software for data cleaning, specialized bibliometric software for
analysis, and graphic design tools for producing publication-quality
figures.
While several established tools facilitate these analyses, they often
present distinct limitations. For instance, VOSviewer [3] excels in the
network visualization of co-authorship, co-citation, and keyword
co-occurrence, yet it lacks text analysis capabilities and requires manual
data importation. Similarly, Bibliometrix [4] offers comprehensive
bibliometric indicators but demands proficiency in R programming.
Tools like CiteSpace [5] and Publish or Perish [6] also exhibit con-
straints, either by relying on manual file transfers or offering limited
visualization and text analysis capabilities. Consequently, none of these
alternatives provides an integrated, zero-code workflow that spans from
Scopus query execution to abstract-level text analysis. Conversely,
programmatic solutions such as the pybliometrics Python library [7]
offer robust API access but requires coding expertise, limiting accessi-
bility for non-programmers.
To bridge this gap, this paper introduces ScopusLit, a web-based
application designed for the comprehensive bibliometric analysis of
Scopus-indexed literature. Developed in Python using the Streamlit web
framework [8] and the pybliometrics API client [7], ScopusLit delivers
an end-to-end workflow. The tool executes Advanced Search queries,
persists results locally, generates over 20 types of bibliometric
visualizations, performs natural language processing on abstracts, and
exports publication-ready datasets and figures. It is specifically designed
to support researchers, graduate students, and authors who require a
streamlined process for producing review articles and comparing mul-
tiple search strategies.

ScopusLit has three distinctive features. First, it consolidates search
execution, full abstract retrieval, and analysis into a single environment,
eliminating manual file transfers. Second, it natively integrates
advanced text analytics—specifically TF-IDF extraction and topic
modeling (NMF/LDA) on abstracts. Third, its consolidation feature en-
ables union and comparison modes via Venn overlap analysis, directly
supporting the multi-query workflows essential to the PRISMA system-
atic review methodology [9].
2. Software description
2.1. Software architecture
ScopusLit is implemented as a single Python file (app.py) organized
into 10 sections. The application follows a functional programming
paradigm with grouped utility functions comprising 74 functions in
total. While this design favors portability and ease of inspection, the
functional nature is friendly to modularization to improve maintain-
ability and scalability. Running the main script starts a local Streamlit
web server accessible from any browser.
The application follows a three-layer separation. The data layer
(Sections 2–4 of the source code) handles all interactions with external
systems, including Scopus API communication via pybliometrics for
searches and abstract retrieval, and local file system operations for JSON
persistence. All API calls are wrapped in retry logic to respect Scopus
rate limits. The analysis layer (Section 5-6 of the source code) contains
pure computation functions that take pandas DataFrames or abstract
dictionaries as input and return processed data structures. These func-
tions have no side effects and no dependency on Streamlit, making them
independently testable. Section 5 covers bibliometric computations
(publication counts, author rankings, citation statistics, and co-
occurrence network analysis), while Section 6 covers natural language
processing (TF-IDF vectorization, topic modeling, word cloud genera-
tion). The presentation layer (Sections 7–9 of the source code) handles
all visualization using Plotly [10] and matplotlib [11], data export via
openpyxl [12] and pandas, and user interface rendering through
Streamlit components, session state, and page routing.
ScopusLit uses Streamlit’s session state mechanism to persist appli
cation state across user interactions, since Streamlit re-executes the
entire script on every widget interaction. Eleven state variables manage
the currently loaded search, cached DataFrames, h-index data, topic
modeling results, and navigation state. Loading a search populates the
search data and its derived DataFrame; loading a consolidation popu-
lates the merged DataFrame and combined abstracts. Each search is
stored as a self-contained JSON file with a UUID-based filename in a
local data directory, capturing the query string, execution date, com-
plete result set, and any downloaded abstracts.
2.2. Software functionalities
ScopusLit implements 20 features organized into five functional
categories: search and storage, bibliometric analysis, abstract text
analysis, search consolidation, and export.
• Search and Storage. Users initiate the workflow Fig. 1 by entering a
Scopus Advanced Search query. To conserve API quotas, ScopusLit
features a "Result Estimation" function that retrieves the expected
document count before initiating a full download. Once executed,
the search results—including all metadata—are saved automatically.
Users can subsequently trigger the abstract download module, which
retrieves full abstract texts incrementally, saving progress every 25
documents to prevent data loss during long retrieval processes or
network interruptions.
• Bibliometric Analysis. Upon loading a saved search, a tabbed
interface provides comprehensive, interactive visualizations of the
dataset. Key analyses include:
○ Timeline and Sources: A dual-axis chart displays publications per
year alongside cumulative growth, while a horizontal bar chart
identifies the top 15 publishing journals. ScopusLit citation anal-
ysis is implemented through the Scopus citedby_count field. The
software computes total citations, mean citations, median cita-
tions, and maximum citations for the retrieved corpus. It also
identifies the top 20 most cited documents, generates a citation
distribution histogram, and plots average citations by publication
year. The software groups publications by year, calculates cumu-
lative publication counts, identifies the peak publication year, and
visualizes annual production trends.
○ Geography and Authorship: Geographic distribution is mapped
using an interactive choropleth world map, alongside top
contributing countries and affiliations. The author tab highlights
top contributors and features an on-demand "Fetch h-index" tool
that queries the AuthorRetrieval API. Co-authorship and collabo-
ration patterns are addressed through both tabular and network-
based analyses. The software extracts author names from Scopus
metadata, counts the most productive authors, identifies frequent

○ Keywords and Citations: Keyword frequencies are visualized
through bar charts and word clouds. Citation analysis provides
distribution histograms, summary metrics, and temporal citation
trends. ScopusLit tracks keyword evolution over time by cross-
tabulating the most frequent author keywords by publication
year and displaying them as a heatmap.
• Abstract Text Analysis. When abstracts are successfully retrieved,
ScopusLit unlocks an advanced natural language processing (NLP)
pipeline.
The text-analysis workflow has three components. First, the abstract
word cloud concatenates all non-empty abstracts and removes a com-
bined stopword list composed of the default wordcloud English stop
words, an added Spanish stopword list, and additional domain-generic
terms such as “abstract,” “study,” “results,” “method,” “research,”
“analysis,” “data,” “model,” “et,” and “al.”
Second, the TF-IDF module uses scikit-learn’s TfidfVectorizer [13].
The default parameters are: max_features=1000, stop_words="english",
max_df=0.85, min_df=2, and ngram_range=(1, 2). Thus, the system
considers unigrams and bigrams, excludes very common terms appear-
ing in >85% of abstracts, excludes terms appearing in fewer than two
abstracts, and returns the top 30 terms ranked by average TF-IDF score
across the corpus. At least three non-empty abstracts are required. Third,
topic modeling is performed on TF-IDF vectors using either
Non-negative Matrix Factorization or Latent Dirichlet Allocation,
selected by the user in the interface. The default method is NMF, and the
default number of topics is five. Users can choose between 3 and 10
topics through a slider. The topic model uses max_features=2000,
stop_words="english", max_df=0.85, and min_df=2. For NMF, the soft-
ware
uses n_components=n_topics, random_state=42, and
max_iter=300; for LDA, it uses n_components=n_topics, random_-
state=42, and max_iter=20. The model requires at least max(5, n_topics)
non-empty abstracts. ScopusLit provides an exploratory interface in
which the user specifies the desired granularity. A lower number of
topics gives broader thematic groupings, whereas a higher number gives
more specific but potentially more fragmented themes. Importantly, the
TF-IDF is implemented in the compute_tfidf_terms(); NMF/LDA topic
modeling is implemented in compute_topic_model() .
• Search Consolidation. To support complex systematic reviews that
require the synthesis of multiple search strings, ScopusLit includes a
powerful consolidation module. Researchers can select multiple
saved searches and merge them in one of two modes:
○ Union mode: Concatenates datasets and automatically dedupli
cates entries based on the Scopus unique identifier (EID), applying
the full Phase 2 and 3 analytical pipeline to the merged corpus.
○ Comparison Mode: Generates comparative visualizations,
including overlaid publication timelines, grouped keyword bar
charts, and a document overlap analysis utilizing tabular statistics
and Venn diagrams based on Matplotlib [14,15] (for up to three
searches) to illustrate the precise intersection of different research
queries.
• Export Capabilities. The platform ensures comprehensive data
portability. Full results and analytical summaries can be exported as
CSV files or multi-sheet Excel workbooks. Concurrently, all
charts—which adhere to a cohesive visual specification utilizing the
color-blind friendly Set2 palette—can be exported as publication-
ready 300 DPI PNG files via the Kaleido rendering engine [16] and
Matplotlib.
User navigation is seamlessly routed through a four-page structure
(New Search, Saved Searches, Analysis, Consolidation), supported by a
persistent sidebar for rapid access to saved datasets.
3. Illustrative example
This example demonstrates and profiles the performance of Sco-
pusLit using the search equation: TITLE-ABS-KEY(("learning
analytics" OR "academic analytics" OR "educational data
mining") AND ("at-risk student*" OR "student risk" OR
"academic risk" OR "early warning" OR "early alert" OR
"dropout prediction" OR "student performance predic-
tion" OR "course failure" OR "academic failure") AND
("predictive model*" OR "risk model*" OR "machine
learning" OR "classification" OR "prediction" OR "ana-
lytics dashboard*" OR "early warning system*")). The goal
of this search was a broad search on analytics applications to quantify
student risk, especially in learning analytics / educational data mining.
A companion video demonstrating the application functionality with
another search equation is also available at the link referenced in the
Code Metadata Table. After inserting the equation, the results estimation
was 1036 documents, whose title information was recovered in 52 s,
yielding a rate of roughly 20 documents/s. Subsequently, abstract
retrieval was conducted in 678 s with 100% success, for a rate of 1.5
abstracts/s. Similar timings were obtained for equations that yielded
larger and smaller corpus. ScopusLit stores the results in a single JSON
format for portability and allows exporting the results in either CSV or
Excel files for easier inspection. The file size for this case was 4.5 MB.
ScopusLit allows a variety of bibliometric analyses based on the infor-
mation stored in the JSON files. Basic ones include the citation count
and the country distribution, as exemplified in Figs. 2 and 3. These two
figures appear instantly on their corresponding tabs once an analysis is
run.
Network analysis is another feature of ScopusLit. It performs co-
occurrence networks of words, countries and authors. For this pur-
pose, it extracts the affiliation_country, author_names and authkeywords
fields from the Scopus metadata stored in the JSON files and leverages
NetworkX Python library to create co-occurrence, co-authorship and
Country collaboration networks. Users can define the minimum number
of co-occurrences and maximum number of nodes. Fig. 4 displays the
word co-occurrence network, which was generated with 6 minimum co-
occurrences and 40 maximum nodes in 13.7 s on an Apple M4 Pro SoC,.
Previous figures were generated using the entire set of search results.
ScopusLit allows result generation using filtered search results. Users
can filter by year range, document types, countries and minimum cita-
tions. Fig. 5 show the results for keyword analysis -word cloud and
evolution along time- when a filter is applied to consider journal articles
and years between 2016 and 2026.
Based on the abstract retrieval, ScopusLit performs text analysis
based on documents for which abstracts were downloaded. On the text
analysis tab, the app indicated the number of abstracts available for the
process. Word clouds (see Fig. 6), TF-IDF and topic analysis. For the
latter, users can select either the NMF or LDA [13] techniques.(Fig. 7)
Fig. 7 shows the topic-word heatmap over the entire search results
using NMF for 5 topics, which was generated by ScopusLit in 2 s. The
LDA analysis yields almost identical results in 3 s. Users interpret the
output by examining the top 10 weighted terms for each topic and the
accompanying topic-word heatmap. The listed terms indicate the se-
mantic content of each latent topic, while the heatmap shows the rela
tive contribution of each term to each topic. The output should be
interpreted as an exploratory thematic summary of the abstract corpus.

Network analysis is another feature of ScopusLit. It performs co-
occurrence networks of words, countries and authors. For this pur-
pose, it extracts the affiliation_country, author_names and authkeywords
fields from the Scopus metadata stored in the JSON files and leverages
NetworkX Python library to create co-occurrence, co-authorship and
Country collaboration networks. Users can define the minimum number
of co-occurrences and maximum number of nodes. Fig. 4 displays the
word co-occurrence network, which was generated with 6 minimum co-
occurrences and 40 maximum nodes in 13.7 s on an Apple M4 Pro SoC,.
Previous figures were generated using the entire set of search results.
ScopusLit allows result generation using filtered search results. Users
can filter by year range, document types, countries and minimum cita-
tions. Fig. 5 show the results for keyword analysis -word cloud and
evolution along time- when a filter is applied to consider journal articles
and years between 2016 and 2026.
Based on the abstract retrieval, ScopusLit performs text analysis
based on documents for which abstracts were downloaded. On the text
analysis tab, the app indicated the number of abstracts available for the
process. Word clouds (see Fig. 6), TF-IDF and topic analysis. For the
latter, users can select either the NMF or LDA [13] techniques.(Fig. 7)
Fig. 7 shows the topic-word heatmap over the entire search results
using NMF for 5 topics, which was generated by ScopusLit in 2 s. The
LDA analysis yields almost identical results in 3 s. Users interpret the
output by examining the top 10 weighted terms for each topic and the
accompanying topic-word heatmap. The listed terms indicate the se-
mantic content of each latent topic, while the heatmap shows the rela
tive contribution of each term to each topic. The output should be
interpreted as an exploratory thematic summary of the abstract corpus.

4. Impact
Bibliometric analysis is essential for literature reviews and is argu
ably among the most transversal and interdisciplinary tool researchers
have at their disposal. It has been applied across disciplines such as
resource allocation [17], engineering education [18] and underground
mining operations [19]. ScopusLit is an open-source tool that lowers the
barrier to bibliometric analysis by integrating search, analysis, and
visualization into a single browser-based interface with no programming
requirement. This makes quantitative literature analysis accessible to
researchers who lack programming skills or familiarity with specialized
bibliometric software. Table 1 compares ScopusLit with established
bibliometric tools across key functional dimensions.
Table 1 compares ScopusLit with established bibliometric tools using
a functional criterion: a feature is marked as supported when it is
available natively within the tool’s standard workflow, limited when it
is available only for a narrower subset of outputs or with restricted
customization, partial when it can be achieved through additional steps,
scripts, or external packages, and not supported when it is not part of the
tool’s documented workflow.
As shown in Table 1, ScopusLit’s main contribution is the native
integration of Scopus query execution, abstract retrieval, bibliometric
analysis, abstract-level text mining, search consolidation, and export
within a single browser-based, zero-code interface. Established tool
such as VOSviewer, Bibliometrix, CiteSpace, and Publish or Perish
provide mature and widely used capabilities, particularly for science
mapping, citation analysis, and bibliometric indicators. However, Sco-
pusLit emphasizes a different use case: reducing manual transfers be-
tween platforms and supporting multi-query, Scopus-centered
systematic review workflows from data retrieval to publication-ready
outputs.
The tool enables reproducible bibliometric workflows. Each search is
persisted as a JSON file that captures the query, execution date, full
result set, and downloaded abstracts. This enables exact reproduction of
analyses and facilitates sharing of bibliometric datasets between col-
laborators. The consolidation feature, with both union and comparison
modes, directly supports the multi-query workflow typical of systematic
reviews following the PRISMA methodology [9].
The inclusion of TF-IDF term extraction and topic modeling on full
abstract corpora represents a capability not available in the most widely
used bibliometric tools. This allows researchers to move beyond
keyword-based analysis to identify latent thematic structures in the
literature, which is particularly valuable for characterizing emerging or
interdisciplinary research fields. From a practical standpoint, every
visualization can be exported at 300 DPI, meeting the minimum reso-
lution requirements of most scientific journals. The multi-sheet Excel
export provides immediately usable supplementary materials for review
articles.

5. Conclusions
This paper presented ScopusLit, an open-source, web-based appli
cation for bibliometric analysis of scientific literature indexed in the
Scopus database. The tool is built on Python with Streamlit and
pybliometrics, and provides a complete workflow from search execution
through analysis and export without requiring programming knowledge
from the user.
The key contributions of ScopusLit are the integration of API-based
search, abstract retrieval, and analysis within a single zero-code inter-
face; the incorporation of TF-IDF and topic modeling on abstracts; co-
occurrence network analysis for keywords, authors, and countries; and
the search consolidation feature with union and comparison modes
supporting systematic review workflows. An illustrative example shows
that ScopusLit can retrieve, store, analyze, and visualize a corpus of
more than one thousand records using a reproducible JSON-based
workflow. The results demonstrate the practical value of combining
API-based retrieval with bibliometric indicators, co-occurrence net-
works, TF-IDF extraction, and topic modeling in one environment. A full
workflow of document and abstract retrieval on a query of 1036 took
<15 min, including figure generation and abstract topic modeling.
The main current limitation is the exclusive dependence on Scopus
metadata and API access. As a result, ScopusLit does not yet support
multi-database retrieval or advanced citation-based analyses such as co-
citation and bibliographic coupling. From a software-development
perspective a future direction is to transition ScopusLit from its cur-
rent monolithic implementation toward a modular architecture, which
would improve maintainability, facilitate testing, and encourage
community-driven extensions and contributions.
